news.title: Trump Voters Give Brutal Verdict on Future of MAGA
news.text:
Republicans are rattled following the 2026 midterm elections bloodbath, and a growing number of them are losing faith.

One in five people who voted for Donald Trump in 2024 are confident that the next occupant of the White House will be a Democrat.

That is according to a new poll, which shows a broad sense of apathy amongst the party after a lackluster first half of Trump’s second term.

Politico polled 2,000 adults in the week after the midterm elections, finding almost twice as many voters believe a Democrat was bound to win in 2028 as those who don’t. 

Only 60 percent of Republicans were still convinced the White House would remain red. 

But Democrats who voted for Kamala Harris in 2024 were exceedingly confident, with 87 percent convinced their party would regain the presidency. 

What nobody seems sure about is who will secure either party’s nominations. With no clear frontrunner from either the Democrats or Republicans, debates and infighting are heating up behind closed doors.

Harris voters are split between wanting a “fighter” (43 percent), a “progressive” (40 percent), or a “creative” (30 percent). 

A surprising takeaway from the poll was that Trump voters are less enthusiastic about competitive politics going forward. 

Only 39 percent want another “fighter,” with 45 percent preferring a “conservative.”

Another point of contention is whether or not their next candidate should come from within Trump’s own inner circle. 

Nearly three in 10 Trump voters said they would rather see someone outside the current administration emerge to win the next election. That support balloons to 46 percent among Trump voters who don’t identify as MAGA. In contrast, 82 percent of MAGA diehards would prefer someone inside Trump’s circle as the next president.

The GOP’s disastrous midterm election results–losing control of both the House and the Senate– completely upended the party’s expectations of what would come next.

Vice President J.D. Vance had long been considered the frontrunner to replace the 80-year-old president, but that future is no longer so clear. And Trump himself has remained coy about who he will endorse. 

Vance is strongly tied to Trump and his near record-low approval ratings, the disastrous war in Iran, and voters massively rejecting the Republican Party and the MAGA movement as a whole.

But Vance has also split with Trump in blaming the midterm results on the war with Iran.

Trump’s own son is facing the same prospects, according to a Reuters/Ipsos survey that asked Republican and Republican-leaning voters to rate a series of possible 2028 presidential contenders.

Donald Trump Jr. would make a “poor” candidate, according to 43 percent of those surveyed. 

Just 12 percent considered him “excellent,” while 17 percent said he would make a “good” candidate.

Republicans on the Hill are growing increasingly vocal in support of Secretary of State Marco Rubio to throw his hat in the ring, but even that is not guaranteed. 

Rubio has publicly ruled out a run for president if Vance announces a tilt in 2028, and insiders have also said the secretary would like an opportunity to step back from politics so that he can make some money in the private sector.

Chair of Michigan’s Shiawassee County Republican Party Dan McMaster said the party needs a candidate who is “as far away from Trump as possible.”

“And even then, I think it’s going to be a battle,” he told Politico.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Daily Beast.

One in five people who voted for Donald Trump in 2024 are confident that the next occupant of the White House will be a Democrat.

news.title: Trump grows frustrated with Vance over Iran war critique, Times reports
news.text:
President Donald Trump has grown frustrated with Vice President JD Vance for blaming the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm losses, The New York Times reported Wednesday.

Trump has told aides and allies that Vance should have said the president was right to go to war with Iran, people familiar with his comments told the newspaper. In private, Trump has praised Secretary of State Marco Rubio and suggested he could be a strong presidential candidate, according to people who spoke on condition of anonymity.

Many Republicans have assumed Vance would lead the field for the 2028 Republican nomination, the Times reported, though Trump has wavered about him in public and private. Trump’s advisers say he is in no hurry to endorse a successor.

Vance wrote on social media the day after the midterms, “The reason we lost is the war.” His lengthy post criticized much of the administration’s pre-election messaging after Democrats won the largest midterm victory for either party since the post-Watergate elections. He also cited the U.S. relationship with Israel.

In the post, Vance said Trump had likewise attributed the losses to the war, although Trump has cited several factors, chiefly his own absence from the ticket. Vance had said when he endorsed Trump in 2023 that Trump would not drag the United States into new wars.

Trump initially told reporters, “I think it's largely true.”

Earlier this month, however, Trump said Vance should have “made one other statement.” “If you had it to do again, would you do it again? The answer is yes,” Trump said of the point he believed was missing from the analysis.

Vance removed from Iran talks

Following Vance’s post, Trump announced that he was removing the vice president from Iran peace talks, which Vance had intensified shortly before the elections. Trump said he wanted Vance to concentrate instead on investigating allegations of fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

On Monday, Fox News asked Vance whether there was any “daylight” between him and Trump. “I think there's no daylight between the president or any other senior member of the administration,” Vance said.

Vance has told Fox News he has not decided whether to seek the presidency in 2028. “We'll figure it out sometime next year,” he said.

His allies say he is genuinely undecided and cite his young family, including his fourth child, born in July. Some allies said a Trump decision to resume major combat operations in Iran would drastically reduce the chances of a Vance run.

Vance canceled a planned Wednesday appearance at the Times’ DealBook Summit, citing Washington meetings to address recent tech outages. The White House did not respond to the newspaper’s request for comment.

Alyssa Farah Griffin, a former White House aide in Trump’s first term and co-host of “The View,” told the Times that Vance’s “daylight” remark “may have seemed insignificant in the moment, but it will live in campaign ads.”

Rob Flaherty, a Democratic strategist and former deputy campaign manager to Kamala Harris, told the Times, “But you do have to feel for him because he's stuck. When you're the vice president, you're stuck.”

Trump praises Rubio

Rubio has had a prominent role during Trump’s trip abroad, while Vance has stayed in the United States. At the Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in Manila on Tuesday, Trump asked, “How hot is Marco, right?” and said Rubio has been “fantastic.”

Rubio told The New York Times earlier that Trump “deserves a tremendous amount of credit” for authorizing strikes against Iran.

A Reuters poll cited by The Jerusalem Post found that 45% of Republican voters viewed Rubio as an “excellent” presidential candidate, compared with 43% for Vance. Completed Monday, the poll had a margin of error of five percentage points for Republican and Democratic voters.

Rubio has said he would support Vance and dismissed reports that he would leave the administration to run for president. Some Rubio allies, however, said he would run if Trump encouraged him.
news.summary: Vance blamed the war for Republican midterm losses; Trump later removed him from Iran peace talks.

news.title: Nearly twice as many Americans think the next president will be a Democrat: poll
news.text:
Nearly twice as many Americans think the next president will be a Democrat after the blue tsunami swept through red states in the midterms. 

Fifty-two percent of Americans think the nominee that the Democratic Party chooses in the 2028 election will take the White House, according to a new Politico poll. Just 28 percent said the Republican Party will take the win.

Just two years ago, Democrats were licking their wounds after Donald Trump beat then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Harris was chosen as the nominee after then-President Joe Biden dropped his reelection bid following a disastrous debate performance against Trump. 

But things are turning around big time for Democrats after they won control of the House and Senate, as well as historic gubernatorial races, earlier this month. While Trump has refused to take the blame for the GOP shellacking, he is facing record-low approval ratings with an unpopular war in Iran, stubborn inflation and an immigration agenda that many find too aggressive. 

Of those in the Political poll who voted for Harris in 2024, 87 percent say the Democrats will win the 2028 presidential election. Meanwhile, 60 percent of Trump 2024 voters say the Republican nominee will take the White House. 

“Whoever’s running for president has seen what’s happened and also has seen the power of our movement, and so this is something that could be carried on to 2028,” Representative-elect Adam Hamawy, a progressive New Jersey Democrat, told Politico.

Now the question is: who will run for president in 2028?

There are several names on both sides that have been floating since before the midterms. 

Forty-five percent of Democrats or Democratic-leaning respondents said Harris would be an excellent or good candidate for the Democratic presidential nomination in the 2028 election, according to a new Reuters/Ipsos poll.

Biden’s former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg trailed, with 42 percent seeing him as an excellent or good candidate. California Governor Gavin Newsom followed, with 40 percent viewing him as an excellent or good candidate. 

Thirty-eight percent of Americans thought Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, a progressive from New York, and Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, who recently won re-election after making headline-grabbing jabs at Trump, would be excellent or good candidates. 

Vice President JD Vance led other potential opponents in the poll, with 62 percent of Republicans and Republican-leaning respondents believing he would be an excellent or good candidate for the GOP presidential nomination in the 2028 election. 

Another 58 percent said Secretary of State Marco Rubio would be an excellent or good choice, and 52 percent said the same for outgoing Florida Governor Ron DeSantis, who unsuccessfully ran against Trump for the nomination in 2024. Thirty-five percent of Americans said Texas Senator Ted Cruz would make an excellent or good candidate.
news.summary: Names that have been floated as possible Democratic nominees include Kamala Harris, Gavin Newsom and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

Vance has suddenly gone from a valued administration surrogate to a cloistered existence, at least for the moment, following his public analysis of the midterms. 

The issue may not be the way Vance linked the midterms to the war, though. The NYT's Tyler Pager misses what may have angered Trump even more than the implicit criticism of Trump's decision to deal with Iran – J.D. Vance's declaration that we must "change our relationship to Israel." To what, exactly? Why would we want to change our relationship with the only liberal democracy in that region and a partner on intelligence in the most dangerous neighborhood in the world? Moreover, Trump's affinity for Israel is well known and has been one of the most consistent characteristics of his foreign policy. Any suggestion that the US distance itself from Israel would have likely offended Trump more than the obvious point about Americans tiring of gas prices and inflation resulting from the conflict with Iran. 

Oddly enough, Pager never mentions that part of Vance's criticism in his analysis. He only mentions Israel in relation to Kamala Harris' difficulties in separating herself from Joe Biden's tepid support of Israel. 

At any rate, Pager believes that the last two weeks have signaled that Trump has chosen Marco Rubio as his most likely successor:

But over the past two weeks, Mr. Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with how his vice president framed his assessment of what went wrong, complaining to aides and allies that Mr. Vance should have made a point of saying the president made the right decision in going to war with Iran, according to people with knowledge of the president’s comments.At the same time, Mr. Trump has continued to praise Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, in private conversations and suggesting that he could be a strong presidential candidate, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe discussions going on behind closed doors. Mr. Trump’s allies have noted that Mr. Rubio has repeatedly said the president’s move to attack Iran was essential for the country’s national security. ...The tension comes at a critical juncture for Mr. Vance, who is considering whether to run for president in 2028, a campaign in which Mr. Trump’s support could be critical to his ability to secure the Republican nomination. The president’s favorable comments about Mr. Rubio are the latest example of how Mr. Trump has been weighing the strengths of the two men as the question of his successor grows more urgent.

Er ... maaaaaybe. Trump has made his irritation with Vance known well enough, although without the usual public broadsides Trump routinely launches against his other critics. He certainly didn't appreciate having to deal with reporters asking him to respond to Vance's criticism. However, Trump's moods are mercurial, while his grasp of his own interests is not. He's married to Vance in the political sense, having chosen Vance as his partner in this term after sharply rebuffing his previous VP, Mike Pence. Trump will spend the next two years as most presidents do with their last years in office: staking "legacy" claims. A public break with Vance would not serve Trump's interests well, especially now that the GOP has to circle the wagons during that period of time.

In the end, the best bet would be that Trump won't pick a successor at all. If Vance or Rubio win the nomination, Trump can claim – legitimately – that his legacy will guide the party's future. If someone else from outside his administration wins it, such as Ron DeSantis, that claim will be harder to sustain, but Trump will have other accomplishments to tout nonetheless. Especially given the midterm results, Trump may well leave the succession question alone lest it backfire on Vance or Rubio. 

In other words, this is but a tempest in a teapot for all involved. Vance has to decide whether he wants to run at all, and in this environment ... it won't be an easy choice.

news.title: Trump grows frustrated with Vance over Iran war critique
news.text:
WASHINGTON — At first, President Donald Trump appeared notably unfazed by Vice President JD Vance’s postelection analysis blaming the Iran war for Republicans’ midterm wipeout.

“I think it’s largely true,” the president told reporters after Vance posted a lengthy missive on social media in which he also critiqued much of the administration’s messaging in the run-up to the elections.

But over the past two weeks, Trump has grown increasingly frustrated with how his vice president framed his assessment of what went wrong, complaining to aides and allies that Vance should have made a point of saying the president made the right decision in going to war with Iran, according to people with knowledge of the president’s comments.

At the same time, Trump has continued to praise Marco Rubio, his secretary of state, in private conversations and suggesting that he could be a strong presidential candidate, according to the people, who spoke on the condition of anonymity to describe discussions going on behind closed doors. Trump’s allies have noted that Rubio has repeatedly said the president’s move to attack Iran was essential for the country’s national security.

Trump has hinted at his irritation with Vance in public, saying this month that the vice president should have “made one other statement.”

“If you had it to do again, would you do it again? The answer is yes,” he said, laying out what he believes was missing from Vance’s analysis.

The tension comes at a critical juncture for Vance, who is considering whether to run for president in 2028, a campaign in which Trump’s support could be crucial to his ability to secure the Republican nomination. The president’s favorable comments about Rubio are the latest example of how Trump has been weighing the strengths of the two men as the question of his successor grows more urgent.

The White House did not respond to a request for comment. Vance’s office declined to comment, pointing to recent interviews the vice president has given.

When asked on Fox News this week about his postelection commentary and whether there was any “daylight” between him and the president, Vance said, “I think there’s no daylight between the president or any other senior member of the administration.”

On Wednesday, Vance canceled a planned appearance at The New York Times DealBook Summit, citing meetings in Washington to address the recent tech outages.

Since Trump brought him aboard as his running mate for a second term, many Republicans have assumed that Vance, a former senator from Ohio, would be the front-runner for their party’s nomination in 2028. But Trump has waffled publicly and privately on his vice president throughout his tenure, and Vance says he has not decided whether to run for president.

“I haven’t made a decision,” he said on Fox News. “We’ll figure it out sometime next year.”

Allies of Vance, who also spoke on condition of anonymity to describe private conversations, say he is genuinely undecided about his political future. They point to his young family (his fourth child was born in July) as one reason he might not mount a White House bid in 2028. They also note his obsession with political analysis and data and suggest that if he does not see a path to victory, he may sit out this race.

The fallout from the war with Iran — and its unpopularity among voters — could be a significant factor, too. Some allies of Vance say that if the president decides to resume major combat operations in Iran, it would drastically reduce Vance’s chances of running.

The vice president, who endorsed Trump in 2023 saying he would not drag the United States into new wars, expressed reservations about the conflict privately inside the administration. But after the huge GOP losses in this month’s midterms, he went public, laying out in blunt terms what he said went wrong.

“The reason we lost is the war,” he wrote in his lengthy social media post the day after the midterms.

Vance made the point of adding that Trump had also said as much — though the president has blamed Republicans’ losses on many factors, chiefly that he was not on the ticket.

For Vance, it appeared to be an attempt to separate himself from the administration’s policy without criticizing the president. But Trump soon announced that he was pulling his vice president from engaging in peace talks with Iran, an effort that Vance had intensified shortly before the elections. Trump said he wanted Vance to focus on investigating allegations of fraud in Democratic-run jurisdictions.

Alyssa Farah Griffin, who worked in Trump’s White House during the first term and is now a co-host of “The View,” said a comment from Vance reminded her of a comment that Kamala Harris, then the vice president, made on the ABC show during the 2024 campaign. When asked if she would have done anything differently from President Joe Biden, Harris said, “There is not a thing that comes to mind.”

“JD Vance is in the impossible position that any Trump VP inevitably ends up in,” Griffin said. “He can’t have any separation or daylight from the president.”

Vance’s “daylight” comment this week “may have seemed insignificant in the moment, but it will live in campaign ads,” she added.

Vance’s allies say a competitive primary, not a coronation, will benefit the next Republican presidential nominee, and they cite Harris’ loss in 2024 as evidence of that theory. Harris quickly secured the Democratic nomination after Biden dropped out of the race, despite some Democrats’ calls for a more formal nominating process.

But Vance ultimately could find himself in a similar situation to Harris, who many voters saw as an extension of Biden, political strategists said. Even as she privately signaled she had concerns about Biden’s handling of the Israel-Hamas war, she was unable to figure out how to separate herself from the unpopular president.

“It’s very hard to get me to say that I have any amount of sympathy for JD Vance because he put himself in this position,” said Rob Flaherty, a Democratic strategist and former deputy campaign manager to Harris. “But you do have to feel for him because he’s stuck. When you’re the vice president, you’re stuck. In the Harris situation, there was not much you can actually do to separate yourself.”

Vance now must wrestle with that complex dynamic as he assesses the future of the Republican Party and in which direction he would try to lead it. His path to the vice presidency — from a “never Trumper” to Trump’s vice president — suggests that he could go in different directions.

Vance was an avowed critic of Trump in 2016, calling him “unfit for our nation’s highest office.” He then became a supporter of Trump and sought the president’s endorsement when he ran for a Senate seat in Ohio in 2022. He received the endorsement and won that race.

Many Republicans believe Vance would need the explicit, or at least implicit, support from Trump to win a Republican primary. But that is far from a guarantee. The president has always relished competition among his aides, and his advisers say he is in no rush to endorse a successor.

And after Republicans’ disastrous results in the elections this month, in which Democrats won the largest midterm victory for either party since the post-Watergate elections, other Republicans see an opening, too. Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas and Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida are among those considering possible bids.

Then there’s Rubio. He has said he would support Vance and dismissed reports that he is going to leave the administration to run for president. But some of his allies said he would run if Trump encouraged him to do so — and Trump has not been shy about lavishing praise on him.

“How hot is Marco, right?” Trump said Tuesday at the ASEAN summit in Manila. “Is Marco doing a great job? He’s been fantastic.”

While Vance has remained in the United States, as the vice president does when the president travels abroad, Rubio is playing a prominent role on the president’s trip. On Tuesday, he addressed public fears about the multiple technology outages in the United States, seeking to reassure Americans that there was no evidence of cyberattacks.

Rubio’s defense of the Iran war, in particular, has earned him goodwill with the president.

In a recent interview with the Times, Rubio said Trump “deserves a tremendous amount of credit” for authorizing strikes against Iran.

“Ultimately, that is the price of leadership — is the willingness to do things that may not be politically popular or expedient but are necessary for your country and its long-term future,” he said.

The distinct approaches of Rubio and Vance underscore a broader debate in the party — should the next Republican presidential candidate align themselves with Trump’s legacy?

Chris Christie, the former Republican governor of New Jersey, who is considering another run for the White House, said Vance’s challenges transcend his unique position as vice president.

“I don’t think anyone that was part of Trump 2.0 will be able to win in the fall of 2028,” he said. “They will be billed as another four years of Donald Trump, and that will not be salable to the American people.”

This article originally appeared in The New York Times.
news.summary:
The tension comes at a critical juncture for the vice president, who is considering whether to run for president in 2028.

news.title: Joe Biden Finally Reveals What He Meant to Say During Disastrous Trump Debate After Infamous 'We Beat Medicare' Blunder
news.text:
Joe Biden has finally opened up about the line he intended to say during his June 2024 presidential debate when he blurted out the fateful gaffe, "We finally beat Medicare," RadarOnline.com can reveal. 

The 83-year-old former commander-in-chief said he knew in that moment that the massive verbal blunder could sink his bid for a second term as president against GOP opponent Donald Trump.Biden Said Debate 'Didn't Feel Right From the Start'Biden discussed the embarrassing flub in his new presidential memoir, Promise Me, America, released on Tuesday, November 17. 

He explained how a grueling travel schedule, including several overseas trips in the weeks leading up to the debate, had left him exhausted. To make matters worse, he began feeling sick during debate prep at Camp David and even feared he might have COVID.

Biden said that after arriving at CNN's Atlanta studios just before the debate got underway on June 27, 2024, "It didn’t feel right from the start," and things only got worse.Biden Meant to Say 'Big Pharma'"One moment was particularly damaging. As I was finishing an answer on the deficit, I lost my train of thought, saw that my time was running out on the clock, and rushed the final part of my answer by blurting out: 'We finally beat Medicare.' What I meant to say was, 'We finally beat Big Pharma,'" Biden confessed about the massive misfire. 

He went on to explain, "This had been a huge accomplishment in my administration. As part of the Inflation Reduction Act, we had secured for Medicare the power to negotiate for lower drug prices. This was a historic achievement that would make life much more affordable for millions."

The former prez wrote, "Ironically, this historic achievement wouldn’t lift my candidacy. It would help to sink it. What should have been a highlight of the debate became Exhibit A that I was too old to do the job."Biden's Debate Was Going Downhill Before 'Medicare' GaffeWhile Biden singled out his infamous "Medicare" blunder as a major turning point in the disastrous debate, he'd also made other verbal slip-ups.

"What I'm gonna do is fix the tax system. For example, we have 1,000 trillionaires in America. I mean, billionaires in America," he fumbled before going on to claim taxes on the uber-wealthy would "raise $500million," quickly correcting it to "billion dollars."

The split screen showed Trump looking on skeptically and trying to understand Biden as he grasped for words. 

"We'd be able to help make sure that all of things we need to...making sure that we're able to make every single solitary person, uh, eligible for what I've been able to do with the, uh, with, with the COVID, excuse me, with, um, dealing with everything we have to do with, uh...look, if we finally beat Medicare," he said.Trump Quickly Hit Back at 'Medicare' SlipAs moderator Jake Tapper turned to Trump for a response, the tycoon declared in a firm and confident tone, "Well, he's right. He did beat Medicaid; he beat it to death, and he's destroying Medicare."

In his memoir, Biden admitted, "I knew I was having a terrible night."

He also criticized Trump for his "refusal to answer questions" and "refusal to accept responsibility for anything."

"Yet none of what he said would generate any impression that lasted past debate night. It would be my answers and my performance that would dominate the press coverage and political conversation in the weeks ahead," the former U.S. Senator admitted. "I left the stage thinking I would be debating Trump once more before the election was over. I was wrong. This wasn’t just the first debate; it was my last one."

After his poor debate performance sparked concerns among top Democrats, Biden officially threw in the towel on July 21, 2024, announcing he was abandoning his reelection bid.

His Vice President, Kamala Harris, rose to the top of the ticket, but she lost to Trump in the November 2024 presidential election.
news.summary: Joe Biden has finally revealed the line he meant to say when he infamously blurted out 'We beat Medicare' during his 2024 Trump debate.
news.author: Beth Shilliday

news.title: Can Democrats Turn a Blue Wave Into a Blue Decade?
news.text:
For many Democrats, the past 10 years of American politics have felt like one long 2016. Donald Trump solidified his position as the decade’s dominant political figure, including during the four-year interregnum that followed his loss to Joe Biden. Then there’s the continual relitigation of the nasty 2016 presidential primary between Hillary Clinton and Bernie Sanders, creating divisions between moderates and progressives that have left the party bickering internally despite being embattled from without. More broadly, 2016 was also the year that brought about a less principled and more authoritarian Republican Party, a hyperconservative Supreme Court, and the decline of American power abroad—an unpleasant asylum we’ve all been living in since.

The ongoing political hangover from that one November night in 2016 may be one reason why some Democrats quickly moved to temper the euphoria that followed this month’s midterm elections. And sure, despite the party’s sizable new congressional majorities, Democrats will probably be able to achieve little of substance as long as Trump remains in the White House. The president may be a lame duck, but his 10-year stranglehold on American life has made it difficult to picture a political universe that revolves around anyone else. More than anything, an earned wariness of imagination explains the collective reluctance to extrapolate too grandly from the results. “This was a repudiation, not a vindication,” Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor and a likely 2028 presidential candidate, cautioned his party.

But sometimes the long view is worth entertaining. And as the dust settles and the final races are called, it’s starting to become possible to discern the beginnings of a path out of our decade-long national nightmare. The depth and breadth of Democrats’ victories have the potential to reshape the presidency, Congress, the federal judiciary, and even the map of the country in ways that could benefit the party well beyond the next two years. Politics rarely offers guarantees; the midterms themselves are evidence of how quickly the political ground can shift, especially for politicians who misread the forces that swept them into office. Yet for those willing to see them, the conditions are there for 2026 to become the year that jump-started a much more liberal and democratically healthy decade, bringing the long 2016 to a decisive end and inaugurating a blue new chapter in American political life. Let’s explore the land of possibility.

Americans are currently not huge fans of what is happening on Capitol Hill. Since 2016, voters have tried almost every conceivable governing arrangement and eventually rejected all of them. We’ve had a Republican president with unified control of Congress, then a Democratic president with the same thing. We’ve had Democrats controlling the House while Republicans controlled the Senate, then Republicans controlling the House while Democrats controlled the Senate. Voters chose to pair a Republican president with a Democratic Congress this time, but it stands to reason that they’ll eventually tire of that arrangement too. As Democratic strategist Lis Smith told Fox News last week, “You rent voters, you don’t own them.” But Democrats’ dominance in this month’s elections have laid a plausible foundation for the party to enjoy a longer-than-normal lease—along with sizable congressional majorities for years to come.

Let’s start with the Senate. Elections are cumulative: If Democrats had failed to defend seats in states Kamala Harris lost in 2024, their incoming Senate majority would be four seats smaller. Likewise, future elections offer a chance to build on this year’s gains. Democrats overcame daunting odds to win 56 seats this month, and 2028 is already looking like the party’s most favorable map in decades. Yes, they’ll have to defend seats in five states Trump won in 2024: Arizona, Georgia, Nevada, Ohio, and Pennsylvania. Yet Democrats have managed to win Senate seats and governorships in each during the Trump era so far. Republicans, meanwhile, will have to defend Senate seats in six states where Democrats just won big—Wisconsin, North Carolina, Alaska, Kansas, Iowa, and South Carolina—and two more, Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats came tantalizingly close. “Some of the very same states where we won this election will offer new opportunities to expand our majority in 2028,” Chuck Schumer, the likely next Senate majority leader, told the Washington Post.

The prospect of holding on to the Senate for multiple cycles matters because it has in recent years been the far harder chamber of Congress for Democrats to win. Some of that is down to the institution’s design, which gives equal weight to rural, relatively underpopulated states that tend to vote Republican. But the good news for Democrats is that Senate majorities, once won, tend to be sticky. Unlike the House, which subjects all 435 members to the will of the voters every two years, only a third of the chamber is up for reelection at a time. That fact insulates many senators from the vicissitudes of politics, meaning it often takes parties multiple cycles to dig themselves out of the minority. After Republicans lost the Senate in 2006—the most recent midterm that took place during an unpopular Republican president’s second term—eight years passed before the GOP managed to claw its way back to a majority. Bigger majorities also take longer to erode, and Democrats just won the biggest majority either party has enjoyed since Barack Obama was president.

Next, the House. Partisan control of Congress’ lower chamber has ping-ponged three times in the Trump era so far, but this year’s results offer Democrats a chance to finally break the pattern. At a projected 260 seats, Democrats’ incoming House majority will be larger than any held by either party in more than three decades. It’s true that many of those seats are in Trump-won districts that could be hard for Democrats to defend in a less blue year. Yet the president and his party seem likely to remain unpopular headed into 2028, which could stem Democrats’ losses. It’s even possible that Trump could continue to boost House Democrats long after he’s out of office. The president has repelled the kinds of suburban, better-educated, and more politically engaged Americans who vote in every election, trading them in for less-engaged, working-class, and rural Americans who are less reliable votes for the GOP in nonpresidential years. If that dynamic holds, it could help Democrats hang on to the House even during bruising midterms that take place under a future president of their own party.

Then there’s the not-so-small matter of what Democrats might actually do with all the seats they’ve won. Expanding their Senate majority to 60 seats or more in 2028 would let Democrats bypass the Republican filibusters that have scuttled bills aimed at expanding voting access and restoring abortion rights after the Supreme Court overturned Roe v. Wade. There’s another possibility too: Even with fewer than 60 seats, Senate Democrats could move to modify or even abolish the filibuster for good as soon as next year. The party publicly debated doing so under Biden, only for a couple of holdouts to block the effort. It’s true that some sitting Democrats, like Sen. John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, continue to publicly support the filibuster, an accidental quirk of Senate procedure that lets a minority of senators blockade bills that lack supermajority support. It’s likely that some of Fetterman’s colleagues harbor quieter reservations too. But a simple majority of senators can effectively rewrite the chamber’s rules, and several incoming Democratic freshmen—including James Talarico of Texas and Annie Andrews of South Carolina—have already said they support some kind of reform.

Filibuster reform is especially important for Democrats. Under Trump, Republicans have largely used their majorities to enact tax cuts and appoint judges, measures that aren’t subject to the filibuster’s 60-vote threshold. But the Democratic Party’s ambitions are tied up in passing big pieces of legislation that will really change things. A Democratic Senate unshackled from the filibuster could be the Senate that acts aggressively to restore abortion access nationwide, expand voting rights, ban partisan gerrymandering, curb fossil-fuel emissions, and pass other big-ticket liberal policy goals.

Importantly, liberal doesn’t necessarily mean progressive; at least for now, Democrats’ majorities are heavily dependent on Trump-won states and House districts. But there may be ways for a durably Democratic Congress to change that too—perhaps by turning Puerto Rico and the District of Columbia into states. Doing so wouldn’t just give nearly 4 million Americans who currently lack voting representation in Congress a seat at the table; it would also add a handful of new senators and members of Congress, who could in turn make it easier for Democrats to win and hold the legislative branch far into the future.

The Presidency

In order to enact ambitious legislation, though, Democrats will need a president who’s willing to sign those bills into law. Lucky for them, both history and the results of this year’s midterms suggest that the party has a very good shot to retake the White House soon—and perhaps even hold it for much of the next decade.

For one thing, Democrats have already won back the presidency once on the heels of an unpopular Trump administration. For another, Trump himself won’t be on the ballot next time. The most recent Republican who tried to succeed an unpopular, term-limited GOP president who’d started a widely disliked war was John McCain, who lost to Obama in a landslide in 2008. Three one-term presidencies in a row have made it hard to remember what it’s like for a single person to hold the Oval Office for eight consecutive years, but in the broad sweep of American history, that’s unusual: Most presidents who seek reelection end up winning. So if a Democrat does succeed Trump in two years, he or she should have a reasonable shot of holding the White House until 2037.

The midterms have also unlocked opportunities for Democrats to improve their presidential odds far beyond that. The most promising is the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact—otherwise known as eliminating the Electoral College. Introduced in 2006, the compact is an agreement among states to award their presidential electors—the 538 people who technically elect the president—to the candidate who wins the national popular vote rather than just the vote in their state. So far, states collectively worth 219 electoral votes (plus another three from D.C.) have signed on to the compact, and Democrats in Pennsylvania, Michigan, Wisconsin, Arizona, and Nevada are already talking about using their new governing trifectas to join it. If they do, the compact will have enough signatories to take effect, essentially sidestepping the Electoral College. That would wreak unknown havoc on how candidates campaign for president, but there’s reason to suspect that Democrats would benefit overall. The party’s presidential candidates have lost the popular vote just twice this century, but the Electoral College has enabled Republicans to win the White House four times over the same period. (Without the Electoral College, Al Gore would have beaten George W. Bush, and Hillary Clinton would have beaten Trump, erasing the past two Republican presidencies.)

There are plenty of unanswered legal questions about whether the National Popular Vote Interstate Compact will pass constitutional muster, and court cases challenging it could become more plentiful if additional states sign on. So maybe the Electoral College will remain—but regardless, the midterms have proved that Democrats have the ability to expand their political appeal enough to win it in novel ways. “The old electoral ‘Blue Wall’ strategy to 270 died Tuesday night,” wrote Democratic strategist Mike Madrid, referring to Democrats’ decades-old stratagem of securing the White House by clinching Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin. “That has been replaced by the new Southern Strategy—California, Arizona, Nevada, Texas, Georgia and North Carolina are the future.” Democrats have yet to win a couple of those states in any Trump-era presidential election, but it’s quite conceivable that they could. The party swept every statewide office on the ballot in Texas this month and won a Senate seat in North Carolina for the first time since 2008.

The Judiciary

Presidents are good for more than just signing legislation; they also nominate federal judges for the Senate to confirm. Thanks in part to this year’s midterms, Democrats are in a prime position to shift the federal judiciary leftward—and to begin to reverse some of the damage that a majority-Republican-appointed Supreme Court has wreaked over the past decade.

Let’s start at the top. Morbid though it is, Supreme Court appointments are for life, so the actuarial tables help tell the story. The court’s oldest sitting justices are both Republican appointees: Clarence Thomas, 78, and Samuel Alito, 76. A third conservative, Chief Justice John Roberts, is 71, and Sonia Sotomayor, whom Obama appointed in 2009, is 72. If any of them were to retire or die in the next two years, it’s likely that Senate Democrats—following the precedent set by Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell, another bitter legacy of 2016—would use their new majority to block Trump from replacing them. Starting in January, Democrats can also do the same to any other lower-court judges Trump tries to appoint during the remainder of his term.

And if 2026 does turn out to be a political inflection point, Democrats will be able to do more than play defense. If the party holds both the Senate and the presidency after 2028 and beyond, liberal justices could end up taking Thomas’, Alito’s, and even Roberts’ seats. That would tip what’s currently a 6–3 conservative SCOTUS in a much more liberal direction, counteracting and potentially reversing the spate of GOP-friendly rulings the court has handed down since Trump became president. A future Democratic president and Senate could do something similar to the federal judiciary writ large, which currently has a relatively even ideological split. There’s also the potential for judicial reform, like instituting term limits for Supreme Court justices or even expanding the size of the court. These possibilities are much more politically volatile—both would be hugely controversial and would almost certainly require sizable Democratic congressional majorities, plus a Democratic president. But they’re already things that ambitious Democrats are talking about heading into 2028.

If you think 2026 was a bloodbath for Republicans in Congress, have a look at the rest of the country. When Trump was inaugurated in 2017, Democrats controlled just 16 governors’ mansions. By January, the party will control nearly twice that number. Democrats are also on track to flip more than 500 seats in state legislatures, erasing the hole the party found itself in after the infamous 2010 midterm “shellacking” that followed Obama’s first two years as president.

The aftermath of that 2010 shellacking is instructive about what may be about to happen now. Back then, Republicans launched a concerted campaign to enact right-wing bills and gerrymander states where they held full control of state government. The party passed anti-union legislation in Michigan and Wisconsin, loosened gun laws in Kansas and Wyoming, and raised new hurdles to voting in Arizona, Texas, and elsewhere. It also drew GOP-friendly congressional and state-legislative maps in Pennsylvania, North Carolina, and other presidential battlegrounds, helping Republicans cling to a disproportionate share of seats even after many voters had started to prefer the alternative.

Now the shoe is on the other foot. According to the States Project, a nonprofit that focuses on growing Democrats’ power in state legislatures, the party is on track to command more governing trifectas come January than Republicans did after 2010. Beyond erasing gerrymanders Republicans drew to advantage themselves, Democrats could attempt to lock in a durable edge for their own party for the foreseeable future.

State legislatures are also responsible for the laws that touch many Americans’ lives most directly. And while some Democrats are wary of misreading the affordability-minded mandate voters delivered this year, the party’s big wins have the potential to unlock a productive few years of liberal legislating across the country. Bills to expand the availability of housing, block A.I. data centers, raise the minimum wage, expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act, fund public transit, protect abortion rights, promote clean power, and more are potentially on the table. “This will be a new era of policymaking that Americans can actually feel,” Mandara Meyers, who leads the States Project, said in a statement. Winning seats at the state level helps parties grow their bench of talent too. After all, the Democratic county councilors, state senators, attorneys general, and governors of today are the potential Democratic presidents of tomorrow.

The Caveats

This vision of our national future is just one of many possible outcomes. If the past 10 years have proved anything, it’s that change is one of the few political constants. And although it may feel as if Trump has frozen our politics in amber since 2016, there’s actually been plenty of churn beneath the surface. Latino and younger Americans swung toward the GOP in 2024, only to swing back to Democrats this year. Democrats have hemorrhaged working-class voters in Michigan, Ohio, and other Rust Belt states but offset those losses in Arizona, Georgia, and the rest of the Sun Belt. We’ve learned that demographics aren’t destiny for either party, and that could mean our politics will get more volatile, not less, as the Trump era comes to a close.

And although the conditions are there for a decade of Democratic dominance, they aren’t self-executing. Democrats have shown an impressive ability to coordinate and compromise in the name of winning elections, but divisive leadership challenges, ideological infighting, and a bruising 2028 presidential primary could derail that cohesion. If Democrats fail to deliver solutions to the high cost of living, voters might decide to chuck them out as readily as they did Republicans this year. Nor are Democrats the only actors with agency: How Republicans choose to respond to 2026 could be just as consequential. So far, few have been brave enough to blame Trump for his role in this month’s historic losses. But the party will eventually emerge from under the president’s shadow, and when that happens, new political strategies could bloom.

In fact, it’s possible to see green shoots already: In South Carolina, where Democrats captured a U.S. Senate seat for the first time since 1998, one longtime Republican aide characterized that defeat to the Wall Street Journal as “the ass-kicking we needed.” A party that’s actually scared of losing is also a party that will tread more cautiously. If the GOP interprets Democrats’ 2026 gains as a repudiation of Trumpism, it may think twice before calling elections rigged, targeting political opponents for retribution, tolerating corruption, or running a figure like Trump for the presidency again.

Those uncertainties aside, the case that a more liberal United States could finally be heaving into view makes more sense the further you step back from the details. For centuries, America has resembled an undulating tapestry of victories followed by defeats, sea changes followed by retrenchments, setbacks followed by renewal. The catastrophe of the Civil War birthed Reconstruction. The Progressive Era responded to the excesses of the Gilded Age. The misery of the Great Depression sparked the New Deal. The tumult of the 1960s gave way to the Reagan Revolution. The Civil Rights Movement grew out of Jim Crow. Obama was succeeded by a man who had denied that the country’s first Black president was an American. So if a much bluer stretch of American politics does rise from the ashes of the Trump era, it would fit a historical pattern that’s been one long, angry decade in the making. Just remember: It won’t last forever.

news.title: Hakeem Jeffries nominated to become first African American Speaker of US House
news.text: Digital Desk | New York, Nov 18 (IANS) House Democrats on Wednesday nominated Hakeem Jeffries to serve as the next Speaker of the US House of Representatives, positioning him to make history as the first African American to hold the chamber's top leadership post when the new Congress convenes in January. According to party tallies from the closed-door secret ballot, Jeffries secured 251 votes with only 11 votes cast against him, facing no direct challenger and overcoming limited opposition from the party's progressive wing over policy issues including Palestine. With Democrats having won 257 seats so far in the 436-member House following their midterm victory, Jeffries is virtually assured of election on the House floor in January, succeeding outgoing Republican Speaker Mike Johnson, who announced he will not seek a leadership role after his party's defeat. While African Americans have previously served as president, Barack Obama, and vice president, Kamala Harris, Jeffries will be the first to serve as House Speaker, a role that stands second in the presidential line of succession after the vice president. Representing a constituency in New York City's Brooklyn borough, where he was raised, the 56-year-old lawyer will hold primary authority over setting the House legislative agenda, budget negotiations, and potential impeachment proceedings. With Democrats holding a decisive House majority as well as 56 seats in the 100-member Senate, President Donald Trump and administration officials will be required to negotiate with Jeffries on federal spending and key legislation, setting the stage for potential policy clashes given Trump's stated opposition to the Democratic platform. Jeffries, who has also voiced opposition to the conflict in Iran, has identified tackling the affordability crisis driven by rising consumer prices as his foremost legislative priority. Earlier this month, he stated that Democrats "are ready, willing and able to find bipartisan common ground with the other side of the aisle as long as we can bring about meaningful change on the issues that matter, and that begins with decisively addressing the affordability crisis". At the same time, sharp friction remains between congressional Democratic leadership and the White House. Jeffries has strongly criticised White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller, his primary administration liaison, calling him a "malignant tumour" and a "dangerous xenophobe and reckless extremist". Meanwhile, Senate Democrats have yet to finalise their leadership for the incoming Congress, with current Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer facing an open challenge for the post of Senate Majority Leader from Senator Chris Van Hollen.

Davis plays a central role in ABC News’ coverage of elections and politics. She co-moderated the only 2024 presidential debate between Donald Trump and Kamala Harris alongside David Muir and was most recently a central member of the powerhouse political team leading “ABC News Election Night: Vote 2026,” building on her extensive coverage of the 2022 midterms and the 2020 presidential election, including all eight nights of the 2020 Democratic and Republican national conventions. Her series “Running Mates” offered another perspective on presidential campaigns through sit-down interviews with the spouses of seven presidential candidates.

Davis’ exclusive interviews have made news across justice, entertainment, history and international affairs. She secured the only interview with Bill Cosby in the wake of dozens of sexual assault allegations and spoke with Jonathan Majors after his conviction on one misdemeanor assault charge and one harassment violation. news.title: ‘I’m not part of Maga any more’: The podcasters who made Trump are turning away from him
news.text:
Just last year, Brett Cooper was being hailed as the conservative answer to Call Her Daddy, the wildly popular podcast among young American women.

The rising right-wing media star, who enthusiastically backed Donald Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, was recruited by Fox News and posted photos wearing Maga hats while horseback riding on her farm.

Now, Cooper is turning down invitations to the White House.

The 25-year-old influencer said she had repeatedly declined offers from Trump’s team to attend events and political roundtables as she grew disillusioned with the president and his administration.

“I’m not part of [Maga] any more,” Cooper said. “I think I’ve moved on.” On her social media channels, which command millions of followers, she has pulled back from political videos.

Cooper’s retreat reflects a broader unravelling of Trump’s once-powerful alliance with podcasters and influencers. In 2024, the president helped define the so-called podcast election, as he won over young men with rambling conversations about everything from cocaine to golf.

The strategy was capped by an endorsement from Joe Rogan, the most popular podcaster in the US, on the eve of the vote.

Now, after a crushing midterm defeat, Trump’s allies are pointing fingers over how they lost their grip on the new media landscape.

Adin Ross, the streamer who presented Trump with a Rolex and a Tesla Cybertruck during a widely watched 2024 livestream, has turned against the president.

“I don’t f**k with any of this political shit any more,” Ross said during a live stream this month, citing Trump’s handling of the Epstein files, the Iran war and rising living costs.

“It sucks that [Trump] sells out to Israel,” he said. “We’ve been lied to as people.” Asked whether he would interview Trump again, Ross was definitive: “No, I would not do it.”

Alex Bruesewitz, the strategist behind Trump’s 2024 podcast blitz, said the podcasters who helped him win had resisted being tied to Maga.

“I have had conversations [with them],” Bruesewitz said. “They said that they hated being labelled right-wing, because they aren’t right-wing.”

The result was that Republicans became reliant on conservative commentators, he said. “We traded Joe Rogan and Theo Von for Mark Levin and Laura Loomer, and that was a bad trade,” he said. “Joe Rogan and Theo Von basically demanded a trade. They didn’t want to play for our team any more.”

A person close to Trump said he did not take it personally. “He’s like, ‘It’s a business. I like these people, they’re nice people, they have big audiences, we did great things with them in ’24,’” the person said.

Another Trump ally who spoke to the president recently said he appeared “in denial” about the scale of the Republican defeat.

A White House spokesperson said Trump was “the most transparent” president in US history and “harnessed the power of new media to cut through the fake news”.

The rupture has raised alarms among the president’s allies, who fear Republicans have squandered the access to younger, politically disengaged voters.

David Sacks, the venture capitalist and former White House adviser, said: “We lost all the podcast bros.”

[ ‘Woke One was crazy’: Why Democrats are leaving the culture wars behindOpens in new window ]

“We should have done a better job staying connected to them ... losing them was a big deal,” Sacks said on his All-In podcast this month, even calling for podcasters to have been given “front-row seats in the White House press room”.

Rogan dismissed the idea as absurd. “How about real journalists!” he said on his podcast. “We’re not press people. We talk shit.”

On Friday, Rogan said the Republican defeat reflected more fundamental problems. “They didn’t just lose the podcast bros. They lost most of the country,” he said, pointing to an unpopular Iran war and the administration’s harsh immigration enforcement tactics.

According to a Trump adviser, the White House failed to maintain relationships with influential podcasters during the president’s second term. Republican operatives were warned in advance of the midterms that the 2024 strategy could not simply be repeated, the adviser said.

The frustrations extend to traditional conservative media. Chris Ruddy, the Newsmax chief executive and a friend of Trump, blamed the White House’s communications operation.

“The messaging was the disaster out of the White House,” Ruddy said, saying administration officials were frequently prevented from appearing on television and podcasts without approval.

A White House official said the administration had maintained relationships with influencers, pointing to creating a seat for “new media” in its press briefings and welcoming Rogan to the Oval Office to sign an executive order in April. They said members of Trump’s administration have done thousands of media interviews, including nearly 1,300 on Newsmax.

[ ‘People are appalled’: How Israel lost AmericaOpens in new window ]

But the estrangement was about more than a failure to keep the podcasters on side. Some of the podcasters say the administration’s policies drove them away.

Cooper said the first big breaking point for her came with the president’s handling of the Epstein files. She recalled reading a Trump social media post suggesting that those demanding answers about Jeffrey Epstein were no longer part of Maga.

“OK, well, I guess I’m not!” she recalled thinking.

The Iran war – after Trump’s promise of no more wars – and the administration’s response to economic concerns compounded her disappointment. “There was a lot of gaslighting that took place,” Cooper said. “It’s just been so belittling.”

Her disillusionment has also affected her business decisions. Cooper said she rejected a paid advertisement funded by a Republican Super Pac in the run-up to the midterms. “The recommended drafted ad copy was like, ‘stop the woke left and these socialists and all of these things, and the Republicans are going to save you’. And I just don’t agree,” she said.

While the Trump campaign has been inviting her to events – with the expectation she would post about them to her social media channels – she has been declining invitations.

“Part of me goes, ‘oh, that would be so cool to go to the Christmas party’,” she said.

“But then I think about what that communicates to my audience and how I feel about what the administration has been doing right now, and it’s just not something that I am really excited about doing.”

[ Democrats pledge to expose ‘absolute avalanche of corruption’ under Donald TrumpOpens in new window ]

She has also reduced her coverage of hard politics and found that her audience was more engaged with cultural and entertainment content.

The disillusionment among influencers has coincided with a broader erosion of Republican support among young voters.

Young men swung sharply towards the Democrats in the midterms, with an estimated 59 per cent of 18- to 29-year-old men backing Democratic House candidates, against 37 per cent for Republicans, according to Tufts University. That was a reversal from 2024, when the same age group favoured Trump over Kamala Harris by 14 points, according to AP VoteCast.

Cooper said her current disappointment did not mean abandoning her conservative values. She voted Republican in the midterms and said she hoped the party would eventually deliver on its promises.

However, for her, the Maga era is over.

“It’s just kind of closing the chapter,” she said. “We’re excited to see what’s next.”

Podcasters who fell out of love with Maga:

Rogan was a stand-up comedian for decades before launching The Joe Rogan Experience podcast in 2009. After more than 2,000 episodes, the rambling, long-form programme remains one of the most popular podcasts. Guests have included Donald Trump, Elon Musk, Kanye West and Edward Snowden.

Brett Cooper

A former child actor and one-time host of the right-wing Daily Wire, her video podcast The Brett Cooper Show has 1.7 million YouTube subscribers. Her podcasts, known for advocating conservative positions, have become less political and more about pop culture, after turning her back on Donald Trump’s Maga movement.

His This Past Weekend podcast was credited with helping Donald Trump win over young male voters in 2024, but he has since bashed the Maga movement. This year he hosted Bernie Sanders, the independent senator from Vermont, and declared that “Bernie is talking about the people I grew up with in the mud”.

Andrew Schulz

The comedian hosted Donald Trump on his Flagrant podcast for a 90-minute interview in advance of the 2024 election. Later, Schulz said he voted for Trump. But recently he accused Trump of “a level of corruption and cronyism that has never been seen in western democracy”. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

news.title: Republicans fret Anthropic IPO will enrich ‘evil’ far-left donors: ‘200 George Soroses’
news.text:
WASHINGTON — GOP insiders are waving a red flag about the Anthropic IPO this week that is about to make its doomsday liberal employees even richer — and have the means to fund far-left Democratic causes and candidates.

The artificial intelligence company that is powering the popular Claude chatbot is going public on Thursday, which will net its seven co-founders, including CEO Dario Amodei, nearly $18 billion each.

“Some of the most evil people in the country are about to get very rich,” one Trump administration official quipped to The Post.

“They are about to mint 200 George Soroses. Only they’re younger, they’re smarter, they’re much more plugged in technologically,” one source well connected to the tech world revealed.

By allowing the IPO to go through, Republicans “are writing our own political death warrant,” the source added.

Dario and his wife Daniela Amodei have donated almost exclusively to Democratic candidates and causes, maxing out donations to Vice President Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign in 2024 and Joe Biden’s successful run in 2020, according to federal campaign finance filings.

Fellow cofounders Chris Olah, Jack Clark, Sam McCandlish, Tom Brown and Jared Kaplan have contributed thousands to Anthropic’s PBC Political Action Committee this year, which has given to both Democratic and Republican campaigns.

The liberal megadonor George Soros and his son Alex Soros donated more than $100 million in the 2026 midterms, helping to deliver Democrats a sizable majority in both chambers of Congress.

Asked what to make of that kind of cash coming from the Silicon Valley nouveau riche, one source close to the White House added: “What could go wrong with a bunch of newly minted centi-millionaire leftists that believe in a radical ideology?”

The AI firm holds ties to the cult-like “Effective Altruism” movement that also urges donors to funnel cash to left-wing causes such as climate change.

Moreover, Dario Amodei in the last election cycle called Trump a “feudal warlord” in a now-deleted social media post and backed Harris to be president.

Based in San Francisco, Anthropic in its early days was reliant on funding from some of the leaders of Effective Altruism too.

Securities and Exchange Commission filings last week showed the AI juggernaut is setting a price range of $70 to $78 per share, meaning the company will at most raise $90.4 billion and hit a $1.4 trillion valuation.

On the Nasdaq, Anthropic will be listed with the ticker symbol “ANT” and start trading on Nov. 19.

Some orders topping $10 billion in shares have already been placed, Bloomberg reported.

The IPO follows the success of tech billionaire Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which raised $85.7 billion in its record-breaking valuation.

That made Musk — who was the largest donor in the 2026 midterm elections — the world’s first trillionaire for a brief period.

A GOP strategist marveled about how much the seven founders of Anthropic will make, not to mention thousands of other employees — but admittedly was not fretting over the uptick in possible liberal billionaires.

“It’s going to be one of the greatest accumulations of wealth in history,” the Republican said.
news.summary: The artificial intelligence company that is powering the popular Claude chatbot is going public on Thursday.

news.title: Fox News Anchor Cracks Up AOC With His Last Question
news.text:
Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) appeared Tuesday on Fox News for the first time since 2020 ― and it sure took a long time for anchor John Roberts to ask her about 2028.

The “America Reports” host waited until the very end to inquire whether she will run for president, cracking up the progressive Democrat.

“Just before we go, 2028’s coming up,” Roberts said. “The DSA wants you to be their candidate. You’ve got to decide soon if you’re going to go.”

Ocasio-Cortez laughed and said, “I mean, my focus is on doing what’s best for people. I’m less about the horse race. You know, these elections just happened. Let’s get some results for people first, and then we can talk about elections later.”

“You’ve got to make a decision by February or March, and that’s just around the corner,” Roberts interjected.

“That’s right,” she replied.

Roberts was referring to the Democratic Socialists of America’s New York City convention voting “yes” Saturday on a resolution encouraging her to run for the White House.

In a New York Times aggregation of recent polls on the Democratic primary race, AOC stood fourth behind leader Kamala Harris, Gavin Newsom and Pete Buttigieg.

Earlier this month, another Fox News host, Kayleigh McEnany, claimed Republicans’ failure to repel socialism in the midterm elections clinched the congresswoman’s decision to run for president.

“I can tell you this,” McEnany said after the Democrats swept the House and Senate. “I believe AOC is sitting at home right now, has made a decision. I believe she’s running for the Democratic nomination. I believe she has a credible shot at getting it. She’s a talented politician. And Republicans, if you’re JD Vance, if you’re Marco Rubio, Ron DeSantis, whoever is out there, you need to be making the case against socialism. If you can’t make it on a Republican debate stage, you should belong nowhere near the Republican nomination.”

Ocasio-Cortez indicated to the Times that she would ponder whether to run for the White House after the midterms.

news.title: Still awaited
news.text:
Michelle Obama, while endorsing Hillary Clinton for president, had famously said of Donald Trump’s brand of abuse-laden identity politics — “When they go low, we go high.” That attempt to capture the moral high ground failed spectacularly as an electoral strategy in 2016. Since then, Democrats tried a range of strategies — some, like Kamala Harris, doubled down on Michelle Obama’s dictum and found themselves roundly rebuffed by the electorate. Others like Al Green, who filed numerous impeachment motions against Trump, and Jasmine Crockett, who matched him blow for blow, also came up short.

The recent results in the US mid-term elections, on the back of Zohran Mamdani’s successful campaign to become mayor of New York, are an important ideological moment in US politics. The answer to Trump’s invectives is to neither go high nor low. Instead, it is to go Left, to its foundations of fairer incomes, affordable gas, grocery and housing, and a supportive State that provides a safety net for all; but — and this is key — to do this without going back to old socialist tropes of classless societies or getting stuck in a quagmire of identity politics and what it means to be American.

Despite massive differences in personal style and campaign priorities, in state after state, Democrats such as the pastor, Adam Hamilton, James Talarico, a teacher, and Abdul El-Sayed, a doctor, made their victories less about Trump and identity and more about a progressive and positive agenda for their constituents. These constituents included Trump’s MAGA base, some of whose frustrations over rising prices and dwindling jobs were deftly channelled away from immigrants and welfare-seekers to large corporations that don’t pay income tax. Taken together, their campaigns demonstrated that there is still purchase for an anti-establishment politics for folks who have been left behind by big capital.

Ten years earlier, Trump had them convinced that the establishment was the deep State in Washington D.C., and that he would be the man to “drain the swamp”. This had sounded promising to many at the time — the increasing digitalisation and financialisation of the economy after the economic crisis of 2008 had left several members of the working class out of jobs. Yet, after six years of the Trump administration across two presidential stints, a self-goal on tariffs, and a shockingly expensive war in Iran, the mid-term results showed that Trump and his acolytes were now perceived as the establishment. The room for someone else to speak for the voiceless against the establishment was up for grabs again.

The political theorist and philosopher, Chantal Mouffe, described the post-2008 crash in politics (primarily in an European context, though it applies more universally albeit at different points of time) as heralding a “populist moment”. With neoliberal policies failing to deliver prosperity in a sustained manner, there is an opportunity for the establishment of new political formations. Such formations could either be more democratic if progressive forces can come together, or, if they don’t, lead to more authoritarian leaders. Her argument is that the time for the old oppositional politics based on either attacking the populist Right for its illiberalism or accepting neoliberal capitalism as the default economic model should now be firmly behind us.

Much of this explains clearly why a result like the US mid-term elections has not happened yet in India or is unlikely to happen soon in the normal course of things. With the rise of Narendra Modi in 2014, the Bharatiya Janata Party captured the political zeitgeist — a disaffection amongst the people with the old elites and their corrupt politics as well as a genuine aspiration for economic growth. The latter demanded quick, visible wins which could only be delivered by large industrialists signing eye-popping MoUs with willing governments, constructing glitzy airports, building eight-laned highways and leading remarkably opulent personal lives, thereby setting an aspirational benchmark for all. For the former, as long as the Gandhi family and other families of state satraps of the erstwhile Congress party remained the faces of the Opposition, Modi could portray himself as the underdog outsider who had made it on his own and thrown out the established elite. Little wonder then that Rahul Gandhi has always been a fixture in the speeches and the campaigns of the BJP.

Twelve years later, the Cockroach Janta Party protests demonstrated early signs of Modi and the BJP becoming the new establishment and the Gen-Z protesters the precursor of what a new Opposition could look like. But neither is there a full-blown economic crisis nor did the protests have a clearly defined political programme. They were righteous and well-intentioned but history has shown that unless popular mobilisation is combined with political institutionalisation, their value diminishes with time notwithstanding their initial intensity. The CJP lacks the organisational apparatus necessary to deliver on this at the moment.

As far as the mainstream political Opposition is concerned, in economic terms they represent the Uniparty — a consensus that growth and prosperity only come through neoliberal capitalism. Admittedly, theirs may be a neoliberalism with shades of welfarism but nothing that comes close to challenging the paradigm. There is simply no economic model that has been offered as an alternative. Maybe the fact that the economy is performing better than most of its global counterparts has meant that the question is premature. But when the time comes, the fact that many among the political Opposition still belong to old political families is further grist to the mill for the present government. Irrespective of what they have to offer substantively, they are susceptible to easy attacks on the grounds of being the old elites who have had their time.

This leaves only two ideological challengers. The old communist parties, on the Left, globally represent an ancien régime failing to make common cause with any ideological cause that is not class based. Without reinventing themselves, they risk becoming a spent force. On the Right, there are the advocates of swadeshi economics — such as the affiliates of the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh like the Swadeshi Jagran Manch and other indigenous associations like the Confederation of All India Traders. Although vociferous in their criticism of large capitalists, particularly those from overseas, they are unlikely to mobilise meaningfully as long as the BJP remains the sole political party in the sangh parivar.

The state of politics and the economy has meant that the time for the populist moment has not yet arrived in India.

When it does, the lack of a clear ideological alternative to neoliberal capitalism will mean that the populist moment is likely to lead to a deepening of anti-elite formations in India. The US mid-terms show how such a formation could, at least provisionally, be made progressive by making the Democratic Party a big tent for a range of protest movements — those out of jobs, worried about grocery bills, anxious about medical care, outraged by Israel, angry about an costly war in Iran — and redefining who is perceived as elite.

In India, neither has the definition of who is elite changed substantially, nor has an economic model been articulated that can build a fairer and more prosperous India for all. The ideological fluidities of Indian politics mean that this moment is a particularly open-ended one with capture possible from a number of different directions. Only time will tell where the chips fall.

Arghya Sengupta is Research Director, Vidhi Centre for Legal Policy. Views are personal
